cards.title: Structural Typing vs Nominal Typing
cards.question: Explain Structural Typing vs Nominal Typing
cards.answer_30s: TypeScript uses structural typing (duck typing at compile time): two types are compatible if their shapes match, regardless of explicit class/interface names. Branded types (`type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: unique symbol }`) simulate nominal typing for IDs.

code.body:
type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: 'UserId' };
const toUserId = (id: string) => id as UserId;

cards.typical_use: Preventing accidental swapping of `userId` and `orderId` strings in function calls.
pitfalls: Remember TypeScript types are completely erased at runtime—always validate external API/JSON payloads with Zod or Valibot.

cards.title: `unknown` vs `any` vs `never`
cards.question: Explain `unknown` vs `any` vs `never`
cards.answer_30s: `any` disables type checking entirely (unsafe). `unknown` is the type-safe top type: you must narrow it with type guards before using it. `never` is the bottom type for functions that never return (throw/infinite loop) or exhaustive union checks.
cards.typical_use: Writing type-safe error catch blocks (`catch (err: unknown)`) and exhaustive switches.
pitfalls: Enable `strict: true` and `noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true` in `tsconfig.json` for real production safety.

cards.title: Discriminated Unions & Exhaustiveness Checking
cards.question: Explain Discriminated Unions & Exhaustiveness Checking
cards.answer_30s: A discriminated union combines object types sharing a common literal discriminant property (e.g. `status: 'loading' | 'success' | 'error'`). TypeScript narrows the exact fields available inside `switch`/`if` blocks, and `never` ensures compile-time errors if a new variant is missed.
cards.typical_use: Modeling API states, Redux actions, and AST nodes cleanly without impossible boolean flags.
pitfalls: Prefer discriminated unions over `{ loading: boolean; data?: T; error?: Error }` (making illegal states unrepresentable).

cards.title: Generics, Constraints (`extends`) & `keyof`
cards.question: Explain Generics, Constraints (`extends`) & `keyof`
cards.answer_30s: Generics parameterize types for reusable functions and containers without losing type safety. Constraints (`T extends object`) restrict type arguments, and `K extends keyof T` guarantees property keys actually exist on `T`.
cards.typical_use: Building type-safe API clients, table components, and state helpers.
pitfalls: Mention `infer` inside conditional types to extract return types or array element types dynamically.

cards.title: Utility Types (Partial, Required, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType)
cards.question: Explain Utility Types (Partial, Required, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType)
cards.answer_30s: Built-in mapped utility types transform existing types cleanly without duplication: `Partial<T>` for PATCH updates, `Omit<T, 'password'>` for public DTOs, `Pick<T, K>` for subsets, and `Record<K, V>` for typed dictionaries.
cards.typical_use: Sharing single-source-of-truth domain types across backend DTOs and frontend forms.
pitfalls: Prefer `Omit` / `Pick` over re-declaring duplicate interfaces that drift out of sync.

cards.title: Type Narrowing, Type Predicates & Assertion Functions
cards.question: Explain Type Narrowing, Type Predicates & Assertion Functions
cards.answer_30s: TypeScript narrows union types via `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, and truthiness checks. Custom type predicates (`val is User`) and assertion functions (`asserts val is User`) teach the compiler custom runtime validation.
cards.typical_use: Safely narrowing untyped JSON responses and `unknown` catch errors.
pitfalls: Be careful with type predicates: TypeScript trusts your boolean return value, so write the runtime check accurately.

cards.title: Mapped Types, Conditional Types & Template Literal Types
cards.question: Explain Mapped Types, Conditional Types & Template Literal Types
cards.answer_30s: Mapped types iterate over union keys (`[K in keyof T]`), conditional types branch on type relationships (`T extends U ? X : Y`), and template literal types compose string unions (`on${Capitalize<Event>}`).
cards.typical_use: Building strongly-typed SDKs, ORM query builders, and route/event systems.
pitfalls: Mention distributive conditional types: `T extends U ? X : Y` distributes over unions unless wrapped in tuples `[T] extends [U]`.

cards.title: Q: `interface` vs `type` — when should you use each?
cards.question: Q: `interface` vs `type` — when should you use each?
cards.answer_30s: A: Both describe object shapes, but `type` can also alias primitives, unions, tuples, and mapped/conditional types. `interface` supports declaration merging (useful for library augmentation) and slightly faster compiler caching on large object hierarchies. Standard rule: `interface` for public object contracts, `type` for unions/utilities.

code.body: type Result = Success | Failure; // Only possible with type

cards.typical_use: One of the most common TypeScript interview questions.
pitfalls: Note that `interface` cannot express union types or conditional types.

cards.title: Q: Why does TypeScript need runtime validation (Zod) if it already checks types?
cards.question: Q: Why does TypeScript need runtime validation (Zod) if it already checks types?
cards.answer_30s: A: TypeScript performs static type checking ONLY at compile time and erases all types in emitted JS. External inputs (HTTP bodies, env vars, `localStorage`, third-party APIs) can still violate those types at runtime—tools like Zod parse/validate at runtime and infer the TS type (`z.infer<typeof Schema>`) from one source of truth.

code.body:
const UserSchema = z.object({ id: z.string().uuid(), age: z.number().int() });
type User = z.infer<typeof UserSchema>;

cards.typical_use: Connecting compile-time safety with runtime reliability.
pitfalls: Using Zod as a single source of truth eliminates type/validator drift.

cards.title: Q: What does the `satisfies` operator do compared to `as` or type annotations?
cards.question: Q: What does the `satisfies` operator do compared to `as` or type annotations?
cards.answer_30s: A: `as` forcefully casts (unsafe). A `: Type` annotation widens the inferred type (losing literal keys). `satisfies Type` validates that a value conforms to `Type` WHILE preserving its narrower inferred literal types.

code.body:
const routes = { home: '/', docs: '/docs' } satisfies Record<string, string>;
// routes.home is still '/' (not widened to string) AND typos are caught!

cards.typical_use: Typed configuration objects and route maps.
pitfalls: Introduced in TS 4.9—great signal of modern TypeScript fluency.

cards.title: Q: What are `const` assertions (`as const`) and `readonly`?
cards.question: Q: What are `const` assertions (`as const`) and `readonly`?
cards.answer_30s: A: `as const` marks an object/array deeply `readonly` and narrows all properties/elements to their exact literal types instead of `string`/`number`—essential for deriving union types from config arrays.

code.body:
const ROLES = ['admin', 'editor', 'viewer'] as const;
type Role = typeof ROLES[number]; // 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer'

cards.typical_use: Deriving union types and runtime validation arrays from one constant.
pitfalls: Remember `readonly` is compile-time only; use `Object.freeze()` if runtime immutability is also needed.

cards.title: Q: What is `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` and why do teams enable it?
cards.question: Q: What is `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` and why do teams enable it?
cards.answer_30s: A: By default, `arr[0]` or `dict[key]` has type `T`, even though out-of-bounds/missing keys return `undefined` at runtime. Enabling `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` types indexed lookups as `T | undefined`, catching countless subtle `Cannot read properties of undefined` bugs.

code.body: // With noUncheckedIndexedAccess: const first = items[0]; // T | undefined

cards.title: Q: How do you type a React component or generic hook cleanly in TypeScript?
cards.question: Q: How do you type a React component or generic hook cleanly in TypeScript?
cards.answer_30s: A: Prefer plain function props (`function Button({ label }: ButtonProps)`) over `React.FC` (which historically injected implicit `children`). Use `ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'>` to extend native HTML attributes cleanly.
pitfalls: Knowing why teams moved away from `React.FC` shows real-world TS+React experience.

cards.title: Q: How do Covariance and Contravariance apply to TypeScript functions?
cards.question: Q: How do Covariance and Contravariance apply to TypeScript functions?
cards.answer_30s: A: With `strictFunctionTypes` enabled, function return types are covariant (a subtype return is valid), while function parameters are contravariant (a callback expecting a broader supertype parameter is safe where a subtype is passed). This prevents unsafe array/callback mutations.

code.body: // Animal[] accepts Dog, Dog[] cannot safely be passed where Animal[] is mutated with Cat

cards.typical_use: Advanced type-system question for senior roles.
pitfalls: Mention `in` and `out` variance annotations (`interface Producer<out T>`) added in TS 4.7.

cards.title: Q: Enum vs Union of String Literals — which is better?
cards.question: Q: Enum vs Union of String Literals — which is better?
cards.answer_30s: A: Prefer `as const` objects or string literal unions (`'asc' | 'desc'`) over TS `enum`. String literal unions produce zero runtime JS code, tree-shake cleanly, and work naturally with JSON. Numeric TS enums also allow invalid numbers unless carefully guarded.

code.body:
const Status = { Active: 'active', Paused: 'paused' } as const;
type Status = typeof Status[keyof typeof Status];

cards.typical_use: Clean bundle optimization and idiomatic TypeScript.
pitfalls: Only use `enum` if an existing codebase or generated schema already standardizes on it.
